questions.question:
A company needs to set up a data pipeline that includes an AWS Lambda function and an AWS Glue job. You have been hired as an AWS Certified Data Engineer Associate to build a solution that has the least management overhead and is fully integrated with AWS services.

What do you recommend?
answers: Set up an AWS Step Functions state machine to run the Lambda function and then the AWS Glue job
Set up an AWS Glue workflow to run the Lambda function and then the AWS Glue job

Leverage Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to set up an Apache Airflow workflow that is deployed on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster. The workflow definition should have the first task as the Lambda function and the second task as the AWS Glue job

Leverage Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to set up an Apache Airflow workflow that is deployed on an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The workflow definition should have the first task as the Lambda function and the second task as the AWS Glue job
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Set up an AWS Step Functions state machine to run the Lambda function and then the AWS Glue job

AWS Step Functions is a serverless orchestration service that lets you integrate with AWS Lambda functions and other AWS services to build business-critical applications. Step Functions is based on state machines and tasks. In Step Functions, a workflow is called a state machine, which is a series of event-driven steps. Each step in a workflow is called a state. A Task state represents a unit of work that another AWS service, such as AWS Lambda, performs. A Task state can call any AWS service or API.

With Step Functions' built-in controls, you examine the state of each step in your workflow to make sure that your application runs in order and as expected. Depending on your use case, you can have Step Functions call AWS services, such as Lambda, to perform tasks. You can create workflows that process and publish machine learning models. You can have Step Functions control AWS services, such as AWS Glue, to create extract, transform, and load (ETL) workflows.

AWS Step Functions state machine represents a simple way to orchestrate a workflow on AWS, as it has minimal management overhead.

Incorrect options:

Leverage Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to set up an Apache Airflow workflow that is deployed on an Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) cluster. The workflow definition should have the first task as the Lambda function and the second task as the AWS Glue job

Leverage Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to set up an Apache Airflow workflow that is deployed on an Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) cluster. The workflow definition should have the first task as the Lambda function and the second task as the AWS Glue job

Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow is a managed orchestration service for Apache Airflow that you can use to set up and operate data pipelines in the cloud at scale. Apache Airflow is an open-source tool used to programmatically author, schedule, and monitor sequences of processes and tasks referred to as workflows.

Amazon MWAA offers support for using containers to scale the worker fleet on demand and reduce scheduler outages using Amazon ECS on AWS Fargate. Operators that invoke tasks on Amazon ECS containers, and Kubernetes operators that create and run pods on a Kubernetes cluster are supported.

Using Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to set up an Apache Airflow workflow that is deployed on an Amazon ECS cluster or Amazon EKS cluster represents a solution with a very high management overhead. So, both these options are incorrect.

Set up an AWS Glue workflow to run the Lambda function and then the AWS Glue job - AWS Glue workflow is only for orchestrating complex ETL operations using AWS Glue, so you cannot have a Lambda function as a component of the workflow. So, this option is incorrect.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/welcome.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/workflows_overview.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/mwaa/latest/userguide/what-is-mwaa.html

questions.question:
An e-commerce company stores customer data in an Amazon Redshift cluster hosted in a private VPC. To safeguard sensitive data such as customer contact details, Amazon QuickSight enforces column-level security (CLS) during report generation.

The company aims to create visual charts of sales rankings by product category and customer demographics. To achieve this, the company's data engineer must configure QuickSight to connect to the Redshift cluster securely.

How can the data engineer meet the requirements in the LEAST amount of effort?
answers: Set up a VPC connection in QuickSight. Create inbound and outbound rules in the security groups for both services to allow traffic between them.

Create an outbound rule in the security group of the Redshift cluster to allow traffic to Quicksight’s IP address. Establish a VPN connection between the Redshift cluster and Quicksight and modify the network ACLs to allow traffic between them.

Create an inbound rule in the security group of the Redshift cluster to allow traffic from Quicksight’s IP address. Establish a Direct Connect connection between the Redshift cluster and Quicksight and modify the route tables to allow traffic between them.

Set up a VPC connection in QuickSight. Establish a VPC peering connection between the Redshift cluster and Quicksight’s VPC. Create inbound and outbound rules in the security groups for both services to allow traffic between them.
questions.explanation:
You can create a VPC connection in Amazon QuickSight to securely access private databases, such as an Amazon Redshift cluster, directly within your VPC. This setup is ideal for scenarios where your databases must be accessible only from certain IP addresses or within a secure environment, ensuring your data remains isolated from the public internet. When QuickSight connects to your VPC, it creates elastic network interfaces (ENIs) to facilitate a secure channel of communication directly to your resources, like a Redshift cluster, without traversing the public internet.

You can connect Amazon QuickSight to the same VPC where your Amazon Redshift cluster is located. Once connected, you'll need to configure the security groups associated with both QuickSight and the Amazon Redshift cluster. The security groups act as virtual firewalls, controlling the traffic that can enter and leave the network interfaces.

In the Redshift security group's configuration, the inbound rule must allow TCP traffic on port 5439 (the default port number of Redshift) from the QuickSight security group, enabling QuickSight to initiate connections to the Redshift cluster. The outbound rule should permit all TCP traffic to the QuickSight security group, allowing Redshift to send responses back to QuickSight.

For QuickSight's security group, the inbound rules need to allow incoming responses from Redshift’s port range, and the outbound rules must permit initiating queries to the Redshift cluster on port 5439.

Hence, the correct answer is: Set up a VPC connection in QuickSight. Create inbound and outbound rules in the security groups for both services to allow traffic between them.

The option that says: Create an outbound rule in the security group of the Redshift cluster to allow traffic to Quicksight’s IP address. Establish a VPN connection between the Redshift cluster and Quicksight and modify the network ACLs to allow traffic between them is incorrect. Establishing a VPN connection is not necessary in this scenario. The use of VPNs is more applicable to scenarios where you are connecting on-premise resources to AWS resources, not for connecting AWS services within the same region.

The option that says: Create an inbound rule in the security group of the Redshift cluster to allow traffic from Quicksight’s IP address. Establish a Direct Connect connection between the Redshift cluster and Quicksight and modify the route tables to allow traffic between them is incorrect. Similar to the other incorrect option, this only introduces complexity that isn't necessary for connecting QuickSight to Redshift. Direct Connect is primarily used to create a dedicated, private connection between your on-premises data center and AWS. QuickSight, being a fully managed AWS service, does not require Direct Connect to access Redshift within AWS.

The option that says: Set up a VPC connection in QuickSight. Establish a networking VPC peering connection between the Redshift cluster and Quicksight’s VPC. Create inbound and outbound rules in the security groups for both services to allow traffic between them is incorrect. While this method is technically viable, VPC peering just adds unnecessary complexity to the given requirement. Since QuickSight can connect to Redshift through a simpler VPC connection setup, introducing VPC peering is not the most straightforward approach. It would be useful in scenarios where a Redshift cluster and QuickSight need to communicate across different VPCs without a shared VPC connection or when cross-account VPC communication is required.

questions.question:
A large-scale data analytics company is migrating their big data platform to Amazon Web Services (AWS). They have chosen to use Amazon Elastic MapReduce (EMR) for processing large datasets and Amazon Aurora as a Hive metastore.

The company’s data engineers need to configure Amazon EMR to use Amazon Aurora as a Hive metastore. This setup will allow the metadata to persist even after the EMR cluster is terminated, enabling cost savings and improved query performance.

Which of the following steps need to be taken? (SELECT THREE.)
answers: Create a MySQL or PostgreSQL Aurora  database.
Modify security groups to allow JDBC connections.
Set JDBC configuration values in hive-site.xml.
Configure the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Set up cross-account access for EMR Serverless and AWS Glue Data Catalog.
Ensure that you do not write to the same metastore table concurrently.
questions.explanation:
Amazon EMR uses an external database to store metadata about the tables, schema, and other Hive data structures. The company’s data engineers would need to create an Amazon Aurora database (either MySQL or PostgreSQL) that will serve as the Hive metastore. This is a crucial step because the Hive metastore is a central repository of Hive metadata. It persists metadata for Hive tables and partitions in a relational database, and provides high availability, and ease of use.

Hive uses JDBC to connect to the metastore database. The data engineers would need to modify the security groups of both the Amazon EMR cluster and the Amazon Aurora database to allow these connections. This is important because the security group acts like a virtual firewall that controls the traffic for one or more instances. When you launch an instance, you can associate one or more security groups with the instance. You add rules to each security group that allow traffic to or from its associated instances.

Set JDBC configuration values in hive-site.xml. This involves creating a configuration file called hiveConfiguration.json containing edits to hive-site.xml. This file specifies the JDBC connection parameters that Hive uses to connect to the metastore database. The data engineers would need to set the appropriate JDBC configuration values in this file to point to the Amazon Aurora database. This is necessary because the hive-site.xml file is where Hive reads the configuration for the metastore connection, among other settings. The JDBC connection parameters that Hive uses to connect to the metastore database are defined in this file.

Hence, the correct answers are:

- Create a MySQL or PostgreSQL Aurora database.

- Modify security groups to allow JDBC connections.

- Set JDBC configuration values in hive-site.xml.

The option that says: Configure the AWS Glue Data Catalog is incorrect because it is not relevant when using Amazon Aurora as the Hive metastore. AWS Glue Data Catalog is an alternative to using an external Hive metastore, but it’s not used in conjunction with Aurora for this purpose.

The option that says: Set up cross-account access for EMR Serverless and AWS Glue Data Catalog is incorrect because it is also not relevant when using Amazon Aurora as the Hive metastore. This would be necessary if you were using the AWS Glue Data Catalog and needed to access it from a different AWS account, but it’s not applicable in this scenario.

The option that says: Ensure that you do not write to the same metastore table concurrently is incorrect because this is just a cautionary step to avoid data conflicts when sharing metastore information between two clusters. While it’s good practice to avoid concurrent writes, it’s not a step in the process of configuring Amazon EMR to use Amazon Aurora as a Hive metastore. It’s more of a usage guideline after the setup is complete. The data engineers would need to be aware of this guideline when using the Hive metastore, but it’s not a step they would need to take to set up the metastore.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emr/latest/ReleaseGuide/emr-hive-metastore-external.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/emr/latest/ReleaseGuide/emr-metastore-external-hive.html

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/migrate-and-deploy-your-apache-hive-metastore-on-amazon-emr/

questions.question:
A company uses an Amazon Kinesis data stream to manage its real-time data processing workloads. Recently, their consumer application on an EC2 instance started encountering ProvisionedThroughputExceededException errors.

The company must resolve this issue to ensure that the read data calls to the stream consistently succeed and that their real-time data processing is not disrupted.

Which actions could be taken to resolve the error? (Select TWO.)
answers: Increase the shard count of the Kinesis data stream.
Implement exponential backoff and retry logic in the application.
Activate the enhanced monitoring feature for the stream.
Enable the enhanced fan-out functionality on the stream.
Use a larger EC2 instance type for the Kinesis Data Streams application.
questions.explanation:
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is a real-time data streaming service offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS). It enables the collection, processing, and analysis of large streams of data records in real-time. A Kinesis data stream is a collection of data records that are continually and sequentially added to over time, much like a stream. Each data record in the stream is composed of a sequence number, a partition key, and a data blob, which is an immutable sequence of bytes. It is capable of handling real-time data from hundreds of thousands of sources at a massive scale. It’s commonly used for scenarios such as collecting and processing log and event data, real-time analytics, and real-time metrics and reporting.

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams uses shards, which are essentially independent streams of data within a Kinesis data stream. Each shard has a fixed rate of data it can handle — 1 MB/sec data input and 2 MB/sec data output. If the data rate exceeds the capacity of the current shards, you will receive a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error. Therefore, increasing the number of shards in your data stream can increase the throughput of your data stream and resolve this error. This is a process known as resharding, which involves splitting or merging shards to adjust the total capacity of the stream.

When a ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error occurs, it means that the application is reading data too quickly from the stream. Implementing a backoff strategy, where the application waits for a short period before trying the request again, can help manage the rate of data retrieval and avoid exceeding the read-throughput limit. This is a common strategy for handling rate-limited APIs and services, and it’s particularly important when dealing with real-time data processing workloads where maintaining a steady flow of data is crucial.

Hence, the correct answers are:

- Increase the shard count of the Kinesis data stream.

- Implement exponential backoff and retry logic in the application.

The option that says: Activate the enhanced monitoring feature for the stream is incorrect because while enhanced monitoring provides additional metrics for the stream, it does not directly resolve the ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error. This error is related to the stream’s capacity, not its monitoring.

The option that says: Enable the enhanced fan-out functionality on the stream is incorrect. While enhanced fan-out can improve the consumer-side experience by providing dedicated throughput per consumer, it does not directly address the overall capacity quotas of the data stream. It's more about optimizing the consumption pattern rather than increasing the stream's capacity to accept writes or aggregate reads without exceeding provisioned throughput.

The option that says: Use a larger EC2 instance type for the Kinesis Data Streams application is incorrect because the size of the EC2 instance does not directly affect the capacity of the Kinesis data stream. The ProvisionedThroughputExceededException error is related to the stream’s capacity, not the size of the EC2 instance running the application.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/kinesis-using-sdk-java-resharding.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/troubleshooting-consumers.html

https://tutorialsdojo.com/amazon-kinesis/

questions.question:
A pharmaceutical company uses AWS Glue jobs to process research datasets stored in an Amazon S3 bucket. The company organizes the datasets by S3 prefixes that represent sensitivity levels such as public, internal, confidential, and regulated. The security team must allow each AWS Glue job role to access only the prefixes that match the job's approved data classification. The team must also restrict access to an approved business-hours window from 8 AM to 6 PM.

Which elements must the company include in a custom IAM policy to meet these requirements?
answers: Use a Condition element with the s3:prefix condition key to restrict all object access and use aws:CurrentTime with DateGreaterThanEquals and DateLessThanEquals operators to restrict the access window
Use a Resource element with S3 object ARN patterns that include wildcards for each approved prefix and use a Condition element with aws:CurrentTime and DateGreaterThan and DateLessThan operators
Use a Condition element with the s3:ResourceAccount condition key to restrict bucket ownership and add an explicit Deny statement outside the approved business-hours window
Use a Resource element with S3 bucket ARN patterns for each classification prefix and use a Condition element with aws:RequestTag to restrict access during the approved business-hours window
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use a Resource element with S3 object ARN patterns that include wildcards for each approved prefix and use a Condition element with aws:CurrentTime and DateGreaterThan and DateLessThan operators

An IAM policy can restrict Amazon S3 object-level permissions by listing specific S3 object ARNs in the Resource element. To grant access only to approved prefixes, the policy can use object ARN patterns such as arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/confidential/* or arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/regulated/*.

The policy can restrict the time window by using the AWS global condition key aws:CurrentTime with date condition operators such as DateGreaterThan and DateLessThan. This allows the security team to limit when requests from the AWS Glue job role can be authorized.

This solution matches both requirements. The Resource element scopes S3 access to the relevant classification prefixes, and the Condition element enforces time-based access by evaluating the request time during IAM authorization.

Incorrect options:

Use a Condition element with the s3:ResourceAccount condition key to restrict bucket ownership and add an explicit Deny statement outside the approved business-hours window - The s3:ResourceAccount condition key helps restrict access based on the AWS account that owns the S3 resource. This can be useful in some cross-account access control scenarios.

However, this condition key does not restrict access to specific classification prefixes inside a bucket. The company needs prefix-specific object ARNs or prefix-aware list conditions, not only an account ownership check.

Use a Condition element with the s3:prefix condition key to restrict all object access and use aws:CurrentTime with DateGreaterThanEquals and DateLessThanEquals operators to restrict the access window - The s3:prefix condition key can restrict prefixes for bucket listing operations such as s3:ListBucket. It is useful when a policy must control which keys a principal can list in an S3 bucket.

However, s3:prefix does not, by itself, restrict object-level actions such as s3:GetObject or s3:PutObject. The policy still needs S3 object ARN patterns in the Resource element to restrict actual object access to the approved prefixes.

Use a Resource element with S3 bucket ARN patterns for each classification prefix and use a Condition element with aws:RequestTag to restrict access during the approved business-hours window - The Resource element must use correct S3 ARN formats. Bucket-level ARNs such as arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket apply to bucket-level actions, while object-level actions require object ARNs such as arn:aws:s3:::example-bucket/prefix/*.

The aws:RequestTag condition key evaluates tags that a request passes to a supported service action. It does not provide a general mechanism to restrict S3 object access to business hours.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/security_iam_service-with-iam.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/amazon-s3-policy-keys.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_resource.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_elements_condition_operators.html

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/techniques-for-writing-least-privilege-iam-policies/

questions.question:
An e-commerce company is experiencing a significant increase in sales during the holiday season. Due to this surge, database queries processing customer orders are taking longer than usual. This is causing delays in the checkout process.

The company’s primary database is hosted on Amazon RDS for SQL server, and the workload is write-intensive. To provide customers with a better checkout experience, the company needs to address the high CPU utilization of their RDS instance.

Which possible solutions can help solve the issue effectively? (Select TWO.)
answers: Identify and optimize high CPU usage queries using Amazon RDS Performance Insights.
Schedule weekly manual reboots of the RDS DB instance.
Add more tables and indexes by altering the database structure.
Transition to a DB instance with greater CPU and memory resources.
Cache the database queries to reduce loading time.
questions.explanation:
Amazon RDS Performance Insights is a useful feature that gathers and analyzes important performance metrics from an Amazon RDS database instance, such as database load and SQL queries executed. It presents these metrics in an easy-to-understand visual format over a period of time to help you analyze your database load and identify any potential bottlenecks. To use Performance Insights, you must enable it when creating an RDS instance. By default, it provides seven days of metric history.

An instance upgrade in RDS is the process of upgrading the underlying database engine or version of an existing RDS database instance. It is important to upgrade instances for the following reasons:

Newer versions provide bug fixes, security enhancements, performance improvements, and new features introduced by the database vendor. This helps keep the database secure and optimized over time.

Upgrading helps maintain support status as database vendors stop supporting older versions after a certain time period.

Future-proofing applications by upgrading to a version compatible with planned features in newer RDS instances or the database engine.

The company should first optimize the problematic queries identified using Performance Insights. However, since this is a write-intensive workload during peak season, upgrading the RDS instance to a larger size would also be needed to scale up the database capacity and meet the demands of processing higher order volumes. Together, these solutions can help improve database performance and provide customers with a seamless checkout experience.

Hence, the correct answers are:

– Identify and optimize high CPU usage queries using Amazon RDS Performance Insights.

– Transition to a DB instance with greater CPU and memory resources.

The option that says: Add more tables and indexes by altering the database structure is incorrect. While indexing can help improve read query performance, it’s not beneficial for write-intensive workloads. In fact, excessive indexing can lead to increased overhead during insert, update, and delete operations, potentially aggravating CPU and write latency issues.

The option that says: Schedule weekly manual reboots of the RDS DB instance is incorrect. Regularly rebooting the database instance does not directly impact long-term CPU utilization trends. While it might temporarily alleviate some issues, it does not address the root cause of high CPU usage.

The option that says: Cache the database queries to reduce loading time is incorrect. Caching is generally more beneficial for read-heavy workloads. Since the database in question is write-intensive, caching would have a negligible impact on reducing CPU utilization.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/USER_PerfInsights.UsingDashboard.AnalyzeDBLoad.AdditionalMetrics.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Overview.DBInstance.Modifying.html

https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/rds-aurora-postgresql-high-cpu

https://tutorialsdojo.com/amazon-relational-database-service-amazon-rds/

questions.question:
An organization collects daily user interaction and app performance logs from its mobile app. Initially, raw logs are transformed by AWS Glue for Spark Jobs and then stored in an Amazon S3 bucket.

Currently, the data in the S3 bucket is stored without any partitioning, causing the Glue jobs to scan the entire dataset during each run.

The company’s Data Engineer has noticed a gradual slowdown in the Amazon QuickSight Dashboard’s query performance over time. Upon investigation, the engineer determined that the long duration of the Glue Jobs is the root cause.

What combination of actions should the Data Engineer consider to improve query performance? (Select TWO.)
answers: Arrange the data within the S3 bucket into partitions by year, month, and day.
Enhance the Glue Jobs query performance by changing the execution class to Flex.
Modify the Glue Job worker type configuration to a larger instance type.
Modify the storage class of the S3 bucket to S3 Express One Zone.
Incorporate the DynamicFrame schema class within your Apache Spark-based Glue Jobs.
questions.explanation:
AWS Glue is a serverless data integration service that makes it easy for analytics users to discover, prepare, move, and integrate data from multiple sources. With AWS Glue, you can discover and connect to more than 70 diverse data sources and manage your data in a centralized data catalog.

You define jobs in AWS Glue to accomplish the work that’s required to extract, transform, and load (ETL) data from a data source to a data target.

You can improve performance just by reducing the amount of data loaded into your Spark cluster for each data source. Consider loading only the data that you need.

To reduce the amount of data loaded into your job when reading from Amazon S3, consider file size, compression, file format, and file layout (partitions) for your dataset.

– Keep the file size of inputs and outputs within a moderate range (for example, 128 MB). Files that are too small or too large can cause issues.

– If your S3 objects are in the hundreds of megabytes, consider compressing them.

– Use a columnar format. Apache Parquet and Apache ORC are popular columnar data formats. Parquet and ORC store data efficiently by employing column-based compression, encoding and compressing each column based on its data type.

– By storing your S3 data to objects in different paths based on how the data will be used, you can efficiently retrieve relevant data. In this scenario, the data is currently stored without partitions, causing AWS Glue jobs to scan the entire dataset on each run. By partitioning your data, you can restrict the amount of data scanned by each downstream analytics application, improving performance and reducing cost.

If your job is taking too much time, but executors are consuming sufficient resources, and Spark is creating a large volume of tasks relative to available cores, consider scaling cluster capacity. You can scale cluster capacity by using the following options:

– Enable AWS Glue Auto Scaling

– Scale-out: Increase the number of AWS Glue workers

– Scale up: Use a larger worker type

Hence, the correct answers are:

– Arrange the data within the S3 bucket into partitions by year, month, and day.

– Modify the Glue Job worker type configuration to a larger instance type.

The option that says: Modify the storage class of the S3 bucket to S3 Express One Zone is incorrect. Although using this storage class can improve latency, it will still not resolve the slow query performance. With this approach, you will deploy your Amazon S3 bucket in the same availability zone as your resources, which will improve the latency. However, it is not mentioned in the scenario if there is a latency issue. This will not resolve the slow performance issue.

The option that says: Incorporate the DynamicFrame schema class within your Apache Spark-based Glue Jobs is incorrect. While this can potentially optimize the jobs’ performance, it is not guaranteed to solve the issue. DynamicFrames are only well-suited for working with semi-structured data formats. It can handle data that includes nested structures or varying schemas more efficiently than traditional data representations. However, the scenario did not mention the complexity of the data characteristics. If your data is already well-structured and does not contain nested structures or varying schemas, the benefits of DynamicFrames may be less pronounced. More is needed if the issue is due to resource constraints or loading a large volume of data.

The option that says: Enhance the Glue Jobs query performance by changing the execution class to Flex is incorrect because Flex execution is simply more suitable for non-urgent or non-time-sensitive data integration workloads, such as testing and one-time data loads. The jobs are running daily, making this solution unsuitable. With Flex, AWS Glue jobs run on spare compute capacity instead of dedicated hardware. The start and run times of jobs using Flex can vary. This solution is for optimizing cost, not for enhancing performance. It could even abruptly stop data processing when AWS takes back the resources.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/tuning-aws-glue-for-apache-spark/reduce-data-scan.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/tuning-aws-glue-for-apache-spark/scale-cluster-capacity.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/components-key-concepts.html

https://tutorialsdojo.com/aws-glue/

questions.question:
A logistics company needs a fully automated solution to check for new records in several operational data stores and process any records that the solution finds. The solution must run every hour and must work with Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Service. Each processing run will handle up to 8 MB of data at a time. The company wants to minimize cost and operational overhead while using reliable error handling.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
answers: Use AWS Glue workflows to run a crawler every hour against Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Service, then start AWS Glue ETL jobs to process all records that the crawlers discover

Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke a Lambda function every hour to check each data store, send processing messages to Amazon SQS when the function finds new data, and use a second Lambda function to process the messages with retries and a dead-letter queue
Run an Apache Spark application on Amazon EMR every hour to check Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Service for new records, process the results, and handle errors in the Spark code
Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to create a DAG that runs every hour, checks each data store for new records, processes the records, and handles errors in Python operators
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Amazon EventBridge Scheduler to invoke a Lambda function every hour to check each data store, send processing messages to Amazon SQS when the function finds new data, and use a second Lambda function to process the messages with retries and a dead-letter queue

Amazon EventBridge Scheduler can invoke an AWS Lambda function on an hourly schedule. The first Lambda function can connect to Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Service to check for new data and create processing messages when it finds records that need work.

Amazon SQS decouples the discovery step from the processing step. The message can contain metadata, identifiers, or pointers to the records rather than the entire dataset. A second Lambda function can read messages from the SQS queue, retrieve the relevant data from the source service, and process up to the required 8 MB working set.

This solution has low operational overhead because it uses managed serverless services. It also has robust error handling because Lambda integrations with SQS support retries, visibility timeout behavior, and dead-letter queues for messages that fail processing repeatedly.

Use Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow to create a DAG that runs every hour, checks each data store for new records, processes the records, and handles errors in Python operators - Amazon MWAA can schedule workflows and implement dependency management through Apache Airflow DAGs. It can also run Python operators that check multiple data stores and process results.

However, Amazon MWAA introduces an Airflow environment, DAG operations, worker configuration, monitoring, and platform-level administration. For an hourly process that handles only a small amount of data, Lambda with EventBridge Scheduler and SQS is more cost-effective and operationally simpler.

Run an Apache Spark application on Amazon EMR every hour to check Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Service for new records, process the results, and handle errors in the Spark code - Amazon EMR with Apache Spark can process large-scale datasets and connect to multiple data sources. Spark also allows developers to implement custom error handling in the application code.

However, EMR is unnecessarily heavy for a workload that runs hourly and processes only up to 8 MB of data at a time. The company would pay for and manage a big data processing environment when a serverless Lambda-based design is sufficient.

Use AWS Glue workflows to run a crawler every hour against Amazon RDS, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Service, then start AWS Glue ETL jobs to process all records that the crawlers discover - AWS Glue crawlers help discover schemas and update the AWS Glue Data Catalog. AWS Glue workflows can orchestrate Glue jobs, crawlers, and triggers.

However, crawlers are not the correct mechanism to check Amazon OpenSearch Service for new operational records every hour, and they do not provide a lightweight record-processing workflow for small data volumes. This design adds catalog and ETL overhead that the requirement does not need.

A global fashion retailer is building a real-time analytics platform for its ecommerce website and mobile application. The company must capture product-view, cart, checkout, and recommendation-click events. The platform must process hundreds of megabytes of events every second and make the data available in Amazon Redshift with the lowest possible query latency for analytics.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
answers: Use Amazon MSK to capture the events, use Amazon EMR to process the data, and use federated queries to access the data from Amazon Redshift
Use Amazon DynamoDB Streams to capture the events, use AWS Glue to process the records, and use a zero-ETL integration to load the data into Amazon Redshift
Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture the events and use Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion to load the data directly into Redshift materialized views

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture the events, invoke AWS Lambda functions to transform the stream records, write the transformed events to Amazon S3 through Amazon Data Firehose, and schedule Amazon Redshift COPY jobs for analytics loading
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture the events and use Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion to load the data directly into Redshift materialized views

Amazon Kinesis Data Streams is designed to capture high-throughput streaming data from sources such as clickstreams, application logs, and user activity events. It can support the ingestion scale required for hundreds of megabytes of ecommerce event data every second when the stream is configured with sufficient capacity.

Amazon Redshift streaming ingestion can read directly from Kinesis Data Streams into Amazon Redshift materialized views. This avoids staging the streaming data in Amazon S3 before loading it into Redshift, which reduces ingestion delay and helps make fresh clickstream data available for analytics quickly.

This solution provides the least query latency for analytics because Redshift can query the materialized views that receive streaming data. The architecture removes intermediate batch loading steps such as Firehose-to-S3 delivery and Redshift COPY jobs, so analysts can work with recently ingested events with lower end-to-end latency.

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/real-time-analytics-with-amazon-redshift-streaming-ingestion/

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/real-time-analytics-with-amazon-redshift-streaming-ingestion/

Use Amazon Kinesis Data Streams to capture the events, invoke AWS Lambda functions to transform the stream records, write the transformed events to Amazon S3 through Amazon Data Firehose, and schedule Amazon Redshift COPY jobs for analytics loading - This option uses Kinesis Data Streams for ingestion and Lambda for transformation, which can be valid parts of a streaming architecture. It also uses Firehose and Amazon S3 to stage the transformed data before loading it into Redshift.

The staging and scheduled COPY steps increase analytics latency. The requirement asks for the least query latency, so Redshift streaming ingestion into materialized views is a better fit than a Firehose-to-S3-to-COPY pipeline.

Use Amazon MSK to capture the events, use Amazon EMR to process the data, and use federated queries to access the data from Amazon Redshift - Amazon MSK can capture high-throughput streaming events, and Amazon EMR can process large-scale data. These services can support complex streaming and batch processing architectures.

Use Amazon DynamoDB Streams to capture the events, use AWS Glue to process the records, and use a zero-ETL integration to load the data into Amazon Redshift - DynamoDB Streams captures item-level changes from a DynamoDB table. It is useful for change data capture from DynamoDB workloads.

The source data in this scenario is clickstream activity from an ecommerce website and mobile application. DynamoDB Streams is not the correct ingestion service for capturing the original high-volume event stream, and AWS Glue plus zero-ETL does not provide the lowest-latency streaming path into Redshift.

questions.question:
A company runs several customer-facing applications on AWS. Each application already writes operational and application logs, and the operations team wants to analyze errors, latency patterns, and user activity across the applications. The team must query and visualize the logs in near real time so engineers can troubleshoot issues quickly from dashboards.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
answers: Send application logs to CloudWatch Logs log groups, stream the log events to OpenSearch Service with subscription filters, and create OpenSearch dashboards
Use CloudWatch Logs anomaly detection to identify unusual log patterns and use those anomaly results as the primary query and visualization layer
Export CloudWatch Logs log groups to Amazon S3 on a schedule by using Lambda, then query the exported log files with Athena
Export CloudWatch Logs to Amazon S3 every few minutes with a scheduled Lambda function, catalog the exported files with AWS Glue, and build Athena queries with QuickSight dashboards
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Send application logs to CloudWatch Logs log groups, stream the log events to OpenSearch Service with subscription filters, and create OpenSearch dashboards

Amazon CloudWatch Logs can collect application logs in log groups. CloudWatch Logs subscription filters can stream matching log events to supported destinations, including Amazon OpenSearch Service.

Amazon OpenSearch Service is designed for search and log analytics use cases. After the log events are indexed in OpenSearch Service, the operations team can create queries, visualizations, and dashboards in OpenSearch Dashboards.

This solution meets the near real time requirement because logs can stream from CloudWatch Logs to OpenSearch Service soon after ingestion. It also gives engineers a managed search and visualization layer for troubleshooting application behavior across multiple workloads.

Incorrect options:

Export CloudWatch Logs log groups to Amazon S3 on a schedule by using Lambda, then query the exported log files with Athena - Exporting CloudWatch Logs data to Amazon S3 and querying the files with Athena can support historical log analysis. Athena is useful when teams need serverless SQL over archived logs.

The limitation is that scheduled exports and Athena queries do not provide a near real time log search and dashboard experience. This approach introduces delay and is better suited for periodic analysis than rapid troubleshooting.

Use CloudWatch Logs anomaly detection to identify unusual log patterns and use those anomaly results as the primary query and visualization layer - CloudWatch Logs anomaly detection can help identify unusual patterns in log events. It can be useful for surfacing unexpected behavior without writing every detection rule manually.

This option does not provide the complete query and visualization solution required by the company. Anomaly detection identifies patterns, but OpenSearch Service with dashboards is a better fit for interactive near real time log analytics.

Export CloudWatch Logs to Amazon S3 every few minutes with a scheduled Lambda function, catalog the exported files with AWS Glue, and build Athena queries with QuickSight dashboards - This option uses several AWS analytics services that can support log analysis over data stored in Amazon S3. Athena can query log files, AWS Glue can catalog the data, and QuickSight can visualize prepared datasets.

This option is incorrect because it creates a batch-oriented pipeline with multiple moving parts and export delays. The requirement is near real-time querying and visualization of application logs, which is better addressed by streaming CloudWatch Logs to Amazon OpenSearch Service with subscription filters.

questions.question:
A global CRM company has recently migrated its technology infrastructure from its on-premises data center to AWS Cloud. The data engineering team has provisioned an RDS PostgreSQL DB cluster for the company's flagship CRM application. An analytics workload also runs on the same database which publishes near real-time reports for the senior management of the company. When the analytics workload runs, it slows down the CRM application as well, resulting in a bad user experience.

Which of the following would you recommend as the MOST cost-optimal solution to fix this issue?
answers: Enable Multi-AZ for the RDS database and run the analytics workload on the standby database
For Disaster Recovery purposes, create a Read Replica in another Region as the Master database and point the analytics workload there
Create a Read Replica in the same Region as the Master database and point the analytics workload there
Migrate the analytics application to AWS Lambda
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Create a Read Replica in the same Region as the Master database and point the analytics workload there

Amazon RDS Read Replicas provide enhanced performance and durability for RDS database (DB) instances. They make it easy to elastically scale out beyond the capacity constraints of a single DB instance for read-heavy database workloads. For the MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server database engines, Amazon RDS creates a second DB instance using a snapshot of the source DB instance. It then uses the engines' native asynchronous replication to update the read replica whenever there is a change to the source DB instance. Read replicas can be within an Availability Zone, Cross-AZ, or Cross-Region.

Creating a Read Replica within the same Region is the correct answer. As we want to minimize the costs, we need to launch the Read Replica in the same Region, because we have to pay for inter-Region data transfer, whereas the transfer of data within a single Region is free.

via - https://aws.amazon.com/rds/faqs/

Comparison for Multi-AZ vs Read Replica for RDS:

via - https://aws.amazon.com/rds/features/multi-az/

Incorrect options:

Enable Multi-AZ for the RDS database and run the analytics workload on the standby database - Amazon RDS Multi-AZ deployments provide enhanced availability and durability for RDS database (DB) instances, making them a natural fit for production database workloads. When you provision a Multi-AZ DB Instance, Amazon RDS automatically creates a primary DB Instance and synchronously replicates the data to a standby instance in a different Availability Zone (AZ). Multi-AZ spans at least two Availability Zones within a single region.

Enabling Multi-AZ helps make our database highly-available, but the standby database is not accessible and cannot be used for reads or writes. It's just a database that will become primary when the other database encounters a failure. So this option is not correct.

Migrate the analytics application to AWS Lambda- AWS Lambda lets you run code without provisioning or managing servers. You pay only for the compute time you consume.

Running the application on AWS Lambda will not help, as it will still run against the main database and slow down the application.

For Disaster Recovery purposes, create a Read Replica in another Region as the Master database and point the analytics workload there - This option is not correct because we have to pay for inter-Region data transfer for the Read Replica, whereas the transfer of data within a single Region is free. Disaster Recovery is not within the ambit of the requirements mentioned for the given use case. The correct solution needs to optimize on cost.

questions.question:
A retail analytics organization has three AWS accounts. A central data platform account owns an Amazon Redshift cluster that publishes a datashare named inventoryshare. Two separate analytics teams in two different AWS accounts need access to the same datashare. A data engineer must grant access by using the Amazon Redshift SQL interface from the producer cluster.

Which command or commands will meet this requirement?
answers: Run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO NAMESPACES '<consumer-account-1>' AND '<consumer-account-2>';
Run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-1>'; and run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-2>';
Run GRANT SHARE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-1>'; and run GRANT SHARE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-2>';
Run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO NAMESPACE '<consumer-account-1>'; and run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO NAMESPACE '<consumer-account-2>';
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-1>'; and run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-2>';

Amazon Redshift data sharing lets a producer cluster grant datashare access to consumers in other AWS accounts. For cross-account sharing, the producer grants USAGE on the datashare to each consumer AWS account ID.

The correct SQL pattern uses the ACCOUNT keyword with each consumer account number. Because two separate AWS accounts need access, the data engineer can run one GRANT USAGE statement for the first consumer account and another GRANT USAGE statement for the second consumer account.

This solution matches the producer-side SQL interface requirement. After the producer grants access, each consumer account can associate with the datashare and create a database from the datashare according to its consumer-side configuration.

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/security-considerations-for-amazon-redshift-cross-account-data-sharing/

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/security-considerations-for-amazon-redshift-cross-account-data-sharing/

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/security-considerations-for-amazon-redshift-cross-account-data-sharing/

Incorrect options:

Run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO NAMESPACES '<consumer-account-1>' AND '<consumer-account-2>'; - Namespaces are valid consumers in specific datashare scenarios, such as granting access to an Amazon Redshift namespace. However, this option uses NAMESPACES with AWS account IDs and combines the values with AND.

The requirement says the two teams use separate AWS accounts. Cross-account authorization should use ACCOUNT with each consumer account number, not NAMESPACE with account IDs.

Run GRANT SHARE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-1>'; and run GRANT SHARE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO ACCOUNT '<consumer-account-2>'; - Amazon Redshift supports the SHARE permission on a datashare for users or roles that need to grant usage to a consumer. That is different from granting a consumer account access to use the datashare.

The consumer AWS accounts need USAGE on the datashare. Granting SHARE to ACCOUNT is not the correct producer-side SQL command for cross-account consumer access.

Run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO NAMESPACE '<consumer-account-1>'; and run GRANT USAGE ON DATASHARE inventoryshare TO NAMESPACE '<consumer-account-2>'; - The NAMESPACE keyword identifies a Redshift namespace GUID, not a general AWS account ID. This option incorrectly places consumer AWS account IDs in the namespace position.

If the producer needs to share with separate AWS accounts, the command must use ACCOUNT. Using NAMESPACE with account IDs will not correctly authorize the two external accounts.

A data engineer has two AWS Glue Data Quality datasets that contain fulfillment information for multiple warehouse locations and operating zones. One dataset is named primary, and the other dataset is named reference.

The data engineer needs to validate that the specific paired values in the warehouse_id and zone_id columns of the primary dataset match the corresponding paired values in the ref_warehouse_id and ref_zone_id columns of the reference dataset. The engineer wants to define this validation by using Data Quality Definition Language rules in an AWS Glue Data Quality job.

Which rule will meet these requirements?
answers: ReferentialIntegrity "warehouse_id,zone_id" "reference.{ref_warehouse_id,ref_zone_id}" = 1.0
DatasetMatch "reference" "warehouse_id->ref_warehouse_id, zone_id->ref_zone_id" = 1.0
ReferentialIntegrity "warehouse_id,zone_id" "reference.{ref_warehouse_id,ref_zone_id}" = 100
ReferentialIntegrity "reference.{ref_warehouse_id,ref_zone_id}" "warehouse_id,zone_id" = 1.0
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

ReferentialIntegrity "warehouse_id,zone_id" "reference.{ref_warehouse_id,ref_zone_id}" = 1.0

The ReferentialIntegrity rule is the correct DQDL rule type when the data engineer needs to compare values in one or more columns from a primary dataset against corresponding values in a reference dataset. In this scenario, the validation must compare the paired warehouse_id and zone_id values from the primary dataset with the paired ref_warehouse_id and ref_zone_id values from the reference dataset.

The syntax places the primary dataset columns first. The reference dataset columns appear second in the format reference_dataset_alias.{reference_column_1,reference_column_2}. This structure tells AWS Glue Data Quality which columns from the primary dataset must be validated against which columns in the reference dataset.

The expression = 1.0 requires a complete match according to the rule response. This means the validation succeeds only when all relevant paired values in the primary dataset satisfy the referential integrity condition against the reference dataset.

via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/dqdl-rule-types-ReferentialIntegrity.html

Incorrect options:

DatasetMatch "reference" "warehouse_id->ref_warehouse_id, zone_id->ref_zone_id" = 1.0 - DatasetMatch compares two datasets to determine whether the datasets are synchronized based on mapped columns. It can be useful when the goal is to compare records across two datasets more broadly.

The limitation is that this question asks for referential integrity between a specific set of paired column values in the primary dataset and the corresponding values in the reference dataset. The AWS Glue DQDL rule that directly represents this relationship is ReferentialIntegrity.

ReferentialIntegrity "warehouse_id,zone_id" "reference.{ref_warehouse_id,ref_zone_id}" = 100 - This option uses the ReferentialIntegrity rule type and correctly identifies the primary columns and reference dataset columns. The column mapping structure is aligned with the intended validation pattern.

This option fails because the expression uses = 100. DQDL referential integrity results are evaluated as a ratio, so a complete match should use = 1.0 rather than = 100.

ReferentialIntegrity "reference.{ref_warehouse_id,ref_zone_id}" "warehouse_id,zone_id" = 1.0 - This option uses ReferentialIntegrity and includes both the primary columns and the reference columns. It also uses the correct 1.0 expression for a complete match.

This option reverses the required argument order. DQDL syntax expects the primary dataset columns first and the reference dataset alias with reference columns second, so the rule does not correctly express the validation from primary to reference.

A retail analytics company uses AWS Glue ETL jobs to collect and process transaction data into an Amazon S3 bucket. The ingestion pipeline writes one small file every hour, and each file is between 250 KB and 350 KB. The company now needs to train a demand forecasting model by processing 5 years of historical data that contains 45,000 small files.

A data engineer creates a second AWS Glue ETL job with the smallest worker type to read the historical files from Amazon S3 and prepare the dataset for downstream analysis. The job runs slowly because Spark creates many tasks for a large number of small files.

Which solution will improve the performance of the second pipeline MOST cost-effectively?
answers: Enable AWS Glue Auto Scaling so the job can add and remove workers automatically while reading the historical S3 files
Rewrite the historical pipeline to compact all files with an EMR Spark job before running the AWS Glue job for forecasting preparation
Increase the number of AWS Glue workers so Spark has more executors available to read the small files in parallel
Configure AWS Glue DynamicFrame file grouping by using groupFiles and groupSize when the job reads the small S3 files
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Configure AWS Glue DynamicFrame file grouping by using groupFiles and groupSize when the job reads the small S3 files

AWS Glue DynamicFrame file grouping is the most cost-effective solution for this scenario. The performance issue comes from processing a large number of very small files, which can cause Spark to create excessive tasks and add scheduling overhead.

The groupFiles and groupSize options allow AWS Glue to group multiple small S3 files into larger logical units when reading the data. This reduces the number of Spark tasks that the job needs to manage and improves throughput without requiring more worker capacity.

This approach directly addresses the small-file problem. Because the input contains 45,000 files, explicit grouping is useful because automatic grouping is enabled only when the input contains more than 50,000 files.

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/best-practices-to-scale-apache-spark-jobs-and-partition-data-with-aws-glue/

Incorrect options:

Enable AWS Glue Auto Scaling so the job can add and remove workers automatically while reading the historical S3 files - AWS Glue Auto Scaling can help jobs adjust worker capacity based on workload demand. It can reduce the need to manually choose a fixed number of workers for some Spark workloads.

The limitation is that Auto Scaling does not directly solve excessive task creation caused by many small input files. File grouping targets the root cause more directly and avoids adding capacity before reducing Spark scheduling overhead.

Increase the number of AWS Glue workers so Spark has more executors available to read the small files in parallel - Increasing the number of workers can add more Spark executors and can help when a job is compute-bound or needs more parallel processing capacity. This can improve some large ETL workloads.

This option falls short because the problem is not simply a lack of workers. The job is inefficient because it reads many small files, so adding workers can increase cost without reducing the task overhead caused by the small-file layout.

Rewrite the historical pipeline to compact all files with an EMR Spark job before running the AWS Glue job for forecasting preparation - Compacting small files into larger files can improve long-term analytics performance. Amazon EMR Spark jobs can perform large-scale compaction when a team needs a separate processing environment.

This creates additional operational overhead and cost. The requirement asks to improve the second AWS Glue pipeline, and AWS Glue already provides DynamicFrame file grouping to reduce small-file read overhead.

A retail analytics company runs a large on-premises Teradata data warehouse that stores merchandising, loyalty, and store operations data. The company wants to migrate the warehouse to Amazon Redshift so analysts can use a managed cloud data warehouse for reporting and forecasting.

A data engineer must convert the Teradata schema to an Amazon Redshift-compatible schema and then migrate the warehouse data. The company wants to complete the migration with the least operational effort.

Which solution will meet this requirement?
answers: Use AWS Glue crawlers to infer the Teradata schema, create matching Amazon Redshift tables, and run Glue jobs for the migration
Use AWS DMS Schema Conversion to convert the Teradata schema, and use AWS DMS to migrate the warehouse data to Amazon Redshift
Use AWS SCT to convert the Teradata schema to Amazon Redshift, and use AWS DMS to migrate the data
Use AWS DMS to migrate the Teradata data first, and rely on automatic schema conversion during the Amazon Redshift load process
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Use AWS SCT to convert the Teradata schema to Amazon Redshift, and use AWS DMS to migrate the data

AWS Schema Conversion Tool is the correct schema conversion tool for this scenario because the migration is from Teradata to Amazon Redshift. AWS SCT supports converting data warehouse schemas from Teradata to Amazon Redshift.

AWS SCT can assess the source schema, convert compatible objects, identify items that need manual action, and help create an Amazon Redshift-compatible target schema. This reduces the manual effort required compared with rewriting the Teradata schema by hand.

After the target schema exists, AWS DMS can migrate data to Amazon Redshift for supported migration paths. This combination uses AWS-managed migration tooling for the schema and data movement work, which provides the least operational effort among the available choices.

via - https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/assess-and-convert-teradata-database-objects-to-amazon-redshift-using-the-aws-schema-conversion-tool-cli/

It can convert supported source schemas to target engines such as Amazon Redshift for the conversion paths that DMS Schema Conversion supports.

The limitation is that the current DMS Schema Conversion supported conversion paths do not list Teradata to Amazon Redshift. For a Teradata data warehouse migration to Redshift, AWS SCT is the appropriate schema conversion tool.

Use AWS DMS to migrate the Teradata data first, and rely on automatic schema conversion during the Amazon Redshift load process - AWS DMS can migrate data from supported sources to supported targets, and Amazon Redshift can act as a DMS target. This is useful after the target schema is available.

A healthcare analytics company runs an Amazon Redshift provisioned data warehouse for regulated reporting. Auditors require the company to retain records of database connection attempts, user changes, and SQL activity that users perform in the warehouse.

A data engineer must configure the Redshift environment so the audit logs are stored outside the data warehouse for compliance review and long-term retention.

Which solution will meet these requirements?
answers: Create an Amazon EFS file system, enable audit logging for the Redshift cluster, and configure Redshift to write audit logs to the file system
Create an Amazon EBS volume, enable audit logging for the Redshift cluster, and configure Redshift to store connection and user activity logs on the volume
Create an Amazon S3 bucket, enable Redshift database audit logging and user activity logging, and configure the cluster to deliver logs to the bucket
Use AWS Config rules to evaluate Redshift cluster configuration changes, and store compliance evaluation results as the complete database audit trail
questions.explanation:
Correct option:

Create an Amazon S3 bucket, enable Redshift database audit logging and user activity logging, and configure the cluster to deliver logs to the bucket

Amazon Redshift database audit logging can record database-level activity for compliance and security monitoring. The audit logs include connection logs, user logs, and user activity logs.

For an Amazon Redshift provisioned cluster, the company can configure audit logging to deliver log files to an Amazon S3 bucket. Storing the logs in S3 keeps the audit records outside the data warehouse and supports long-term retention and independent review.

The user activity log requires the associated database parameter to be enabled. Therefore, enabling Redshift audit logging, enabling user activity logging, and choosing an S3 bucket as the destination meets the requirement to store user activity and connection activity logs.

Incorrect options:

Create an Amazon EFS file system, enable audit logging for the Redshift cluster, and configure Redshift to write audit logs to the file system - Amazon EFS provides shared file storage that can be mounted by supported compute services. It is useful for workloads that need a managed network file system.

This option does not meet the requirement because Amazon Redshift audit logging does not write audit logs to an EFS file system. Redshift supports audit log delivery to destinations such as Amazon S3 for provisioned clusters.

Use AWS Config rules to evaluate Redshift cluster configuration changes, and store compliance evaluation results as the complete database audit trail - AWS Config can evaluate resource configuration against rules and record configuration changes. It is useful for checking whether Redshift clusters meet governance requirements.

This does not provide a complete audit trail of database connections and user SQL activity. AWS Config evaluates configuration compliance, while Redshift database audit logging captures the required user and connection activity logs.

Create an Amazon EBS volume, enable audit logging for the Redshift cluster, and configure Redshift to store connection and user activity logs on the volume - Amazon EBS provides block storage for EC2 instances. EBS volumes can support applications that run on EC2 and need persistent local block storage.

This option falls short because Amazon Redshift is a managed data warehouse service. The data engineer does not attach an EBS volume to a Redshift cluster to store audit logs.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/db-auditing.html

https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/redshift-audit-logging

questions.question:
A data engineering team manages 10 TB of data in an Amazon S3 bucket. The team must meet new data lifecycle and retention policies. Under the new guidelines, all newly stored data must be readily available for random, occasional SQL queries. Data older than 3 years requires secure storage but must be accessible within 8 hours for compliance audits. Additionally, data exceeding a 10-year retention period should be permanently deleted. The team initially explored using a tumbling window for real-time analytics but determined that occasional SQL queries made a simpler, cost-effective approach more appropriate.

Which solution will fulfill this requirement most cost-effectively?
answers: Configure the new data to be stored in the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Use Amazon Athena for ad-hoc querying. Implement lifecycle rules for data archival to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 3 years and deletion after 10 years.

Set the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for new data with a configuration towards Deep Archive Access for longer-term storage. Utilize Amazon Athena for ad-hoc querying. Configure S3 Intelligent Tiering to purge data after 10 years.

Use Amazon Redshift for data storage of the new data, then configure Redshift Spectrum to directly query data on S3. Implement lifecycle rules for data archival to the Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class. Set up another lifecycle rule to delete data longer than 10 years.

Configure Amazon RDS to store the newly added data. Create an Amazon Lambda function to periodically export the snapshots to the S3 Standard class. Set up lifecycle policies for transferring snapshots to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 3 years and deleting data after 10 years.
questions.explanation:
Amazon S3 offers different types of storage classes that users can choose based on the specific needs of their workload. Depending on their workload's data access, resiliency, and performance requirements, these classes are tailored to provide the best storage options at the lowest possible costs. S3 storage classes are versatile and suitable for nearly any use case - including those with high-performance demands, data lakes, residency requirements, unknown or changing access patterns, or archival storage.

One of these classes is the Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA). Amazon S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class is designed for data that is accessed less frequently but, when needed, requires rapid access. S3 Standard-IA offers the high durability, throughput, and low latency of S3 Standard but with a lower storage cost and a slightly higher retrieval fee. This storage class makes it an ideal solution for long-term storage and backups and a data store for disaster recovery files. Amazon Athena allows users to analyze data stored in Amazon S3 with SQL queries. It's interactive and serverless, so there's no infrastructure to manage. Users are charged only for the queries they run, making it an incredibly cost-effective solution.

By implementing lifecycle rules in Amazon S3, you can easily manage your data throughout its lifecycle. S3 Lifecycle configuration rules allow you to transition objects to more cost-effective storage classes, such as S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive, for long-term storage and archiving purposes. Moreover, you have the option to set up rules that will automatically delete objects after a specific period, which helps you comply with data governance and regulatory requirements.

Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, previously known as S3 Glacier, is a cost-effective storage solution for archiving data. You can configure retrieval times from minutes to hours, which is suitable for accessing data for compliance audits within a 10-hour window. On the other hand, the S3 Glacier Deep Archive is designed for data that is accessed less frequently but needs to be retained for decades as part of digital preservation or regulatory compliance. It is the most affordable long-term archiving storage option available on AWS.

Hence, the correct answer is: Configure the new data to be stored in the S3 Standard-Infrequent Access (S3 Standard-IA) storage class. Use Amazon Athena for ad-hoc querying. Implement lifecycle rules for data archival to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 3 years and deletion after 10 years.

The option that says: Set the S3 Intelligent-Tiering storage class for new data with a configuration towards Deep Archive Access for longer-term storage. Utilize Amazon Athena for ad-hoc querying. Configure S3 Intelligent Tiering to purge data after 10 years is incorrect. Although using Amazon Athena to query data meets one of the requirements, transitioning to Deep Archive Access makes it impossible for data to be accessible within an 8-hour window. S3 Glacier Deep Archive is intended for long-term data storage that is accessed once or twice a year, with retrieval times typically ranging from 12 to 48 hours.

The option that says: Use Amazon Redshift for data storage of the new data, then configure Redshift Spectrum to directly query data on S3. Implement lifecycle rules for data archival to the Amazon S3 Glacier Deep Archive storage class. Set up another lifecycle rule to delete data longer than 10 years is incorrect. Redshift is primarily a data warehousing solution for large-scale analytical workloads, not occasional SQL queries on recently ingested data. While Redshift Spectrum allows querying data in S3, maintaining a Redshift cluster incurs hourly charges, making it a less cost-effective solution. Moreover, although S3 Glacier Deep Archive is cheaper than Glacier Flexible Retrieval, it only allows retrieval times ranging from 12 to 48 hours.

The option that says: Configure Amazon RDS to store the newly added data. Create an Amazon Lambda function to periodically export the snapshots to the S3 Standard class. Set up lifecycle policies for transferring snapshots to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval after 3 years and deleting data after 10 years is incorrect. Amazon RDS is primarily a database service for relational databases and is not optimized for cost-effective data storage and retrieval for compliance and lifecycle management in the way S3 and its associated services are. Moreover, managing snapshots and exports introduces operational overhead that does not directly contribute to the goals of easy SQL analysis and compliance with lifecycle policies.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/storage-class-intro.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/backup-recovery/amazon-s3-glacier.html

questions.question:
A data engineering team manages an Amazon DynamoDB table configured with provisioned capacity mode. The table uses a primary key to uniquely identify the items stored by the application. The table experiences a highly predictable traffic pattern, with peaks occurring at midnight every day. These peaks are followed by a period of low activity in the morning, which gradually transitions to normal levels for the remainder of the day.

The data engineering team wants to maintain the application's performance during peak times and save costs during low usage periods.

Which solution meets this requirement?
answers: Set the provisioned capacity to match the highest observed demand during peak periods.
Update the table’s class to DynamoDB Standard Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA).
Update the table’s capacity to use AWS Application Auto Scaling based on minimum and maximum utilization.
Switch to an on-demand capacity mode for the table.
questions.explanation:
Amazon DynamoDB allows for two capacity modes for managing throughput costs: provisioned and on-demand. In provisioned capacity mode, the user specifies the number of reads and writes per second as required by the application. This mode is cost-effective for predictable workloads where the throughput does not frequently change. On-demand capacity mode, on the other hand, offers flexible billing and automatically accommodates the table's workload without requiring manual scaling.

AWS Application Auto Scaling enables automatic adjustment of resources to maintain consistent, predictable performance at the lowest possible cost. It supports scheduling, which allows for capacity planning based on known usage patterns. This feature is particularly useful for applications with predictable load patterns.

Implementing AWS Application Auto Scaling for DynamoDB allows for the dynamic adjustment of provisioned capacity to align with the application’s workload patterns, ensuring high performance during peak times and cost savings during off-peak times. This approach leverages the predictable nature of the workload, enhancing resource utilization efficiency without the need for manual intervention or the costs associated with maintaining excessive provisioned capacity.

Hence, the correct answer is: Update the table’s capacity to use AWS Application Auto Scaling based on minimum and maximum utilization.

The option that says: Set the provisioned capacity to match the highest observed demand during peak periods is incorrect. In a provisioned capacity mode, you pay for the specified capacity regardless of actual usage. Therefore, matching capacity to peak demand without adjusting for periods of low activity only results in paying for unneeded capacity during those lower periods, which is not cost-effective.

The option that says: Update the table’s class to DynamoDB Standard Infrequent Access (DynamoDB Standard-IA) is incorrect. DynamoDB Standard-IA is primarily used in scenarios where data is accessed less frequently, offering lower storage costs while maintaining the same performance levels as the standard storage class. However, reading from and writing to these tables costs more than the Standard class, making it pricier for tables that are frequently used, such as the one in the scenario.

The option that says: Switch to an on-demand capacity mode for the table is incorrect. The on-demand capacity mode charges for each read or write, unlike the provisioned mode, where you pay for a set capacity. For tables with predictable traffic, using provisioned capacity often works out cheaper. This is because you can set your capacity to cover the expected throughput, avoiding the costs tied to the per-action pricing of the on-demand mode.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/AutoScaling.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/what-is-application-auto-scaling.html
