questions.question:
A data engineer is trying to use AWS Glue Interactive Sessions in Amazon SageMaker Studio for data preparation tasks. The data engineer has successfully created a SageMaker IAM role with trust policies for both SageMaker and Glue services. The interactive session is being incorporated into an ML workflow that prepares data for subsequent analytical tasks. Despite this setup, the data engineer is being denied access when attempting to initiate an Glue Interactive Session.

How can the data engineer resolve the issue?
answers: Attach the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy to the SageMaker’s execution role.
Attach the AwsGlueSessionUserRestrictedServiceRole managed policy to the SageMaker’s execution role.
Ensure the data engineer's IAM user has permission to perform the sts:AssumeRole and sagemaker:AddAssociation actions.
Add the AWSGlueServiceRole managed policy to the IAM user of the data engineer.
questions.explanation:
Amazon SageMaker Studio is an integrated development environment (IDE) for machine learning that provides every tool needed to build, train, and deploy machine learning models. SageMaker offers a user-friendly interface for executing ML workflows, making its tools accessible across various integrated development environments (IDEs). Additionally, It conducts operations on your behalf by leveraging other AWS services. You need to assign permissions to enable SageMaker to utilize these services and access the corresponding resources. This permission is achieved through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role, granting SageMaker the necessary permissions.

AWS Glue Interactive Sessions provides a programmatic and visual interface for building and testing ETL scripts for data preparation. To use it in Amazon SageMaker Studio, the SageMaker execution role needs to have the necessary permissions for AWS Glue. This can be achieved by attaching the AwsGlueSessionUserRestrictedServiceRole managed policy to the SageMaker execution role.

The AwsGlueSessionUserRestrictedServiceRole policy grants the required permissions for creating and managing AWS Glue Interactive Sessions, as well as accessing the AWS Glue Data Catalog and other related resources.

Hence, the correct answer is: Attach the AwsGlueSessionUserRestrictedServiceRole managed policy to the SageMaker’s execution role.

The option that says:  Attach the AmazonSageMakerFullAccess managed policy to the SageMaker’s execution role. is incorrect. This policy just grants all actions across Amazon SageMaker, which is not required for the specific task of using AWS Glue Interactive Sessions.

The option that says: Ensure the data engineer's IAM user has permission to perform the sts:AssumeRole and sagemaker:AddAssociation actions is incorrect. While sts:AssumeRole is required to assume an IAM role, this permission is not specifically needed for using AWS Glue Interactive Sessions. Additionally, the sagemaker:AddAssociation permission is only used for associating resources with a SageMaker notebook instance or studio, but it's not directly related to AWS Glue Interactive Sessions.

The option that says: Add the AWSGlueServiceRole managed policy to the IAM user of the data engineer is incorrect because this policy is typically used to grant AWS Glue the permissions it needs to execute jobs and does not apply to the SageMaker execution role's permissions for AWS Glue Interactive Sessions.

 

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/getting-started-glue-sm.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/sagemaker-roles.html

questions.question:
A data engineer is assigned to build a data lake for a company’s business data stored on Amazon S3. The data, saved in the Apache Parquet format, will be utilized for complex analytic tasks. The company anticipates that users will need granular access to the datasets.

Which of the following will meet these requirements in the shortest amount of time and in the MOST cost-effective manner?
answers: Execute an AWS Glue crawler to establish a data catalog for existing data and register its Amazon S3 path location on Lake Formation. For data security, allocate granular permissions to various users.
Leverage Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) to orchestrate and schedule data processing workflows. Ensure data security by assigning appropriate access controls.
Using AWS Lake Formation, register the S3 bucket where the data resides. To secure the data, assign granular permissions to different users.
Import data from Amazon S3 using an AWS Lake Formation blueprint. Subsequently, accord users granular Lake Formation permissions as needed.
questions.explanation:
AWS Lake Formation is a service that makes it easy to set up a secure data lake in days. A data lake is a centralized, curated, and secured repository that stores all your data, both in its original form and prepared for analysis. A data lake enables you to break down data silos and combine different types of analytics to gain insights and guide better business decisions.

Amazon S3 forms the storage layer for Lake Formation. If you already use S3, you typically begin by registering existing S3 buckets that contain your data. Lake Formation creates new buckets for the data lake and imports data into them. AWS always stores this data in your account, and only you have direct access to it.

AWS Lake Formation is integrated with AWS Glue, which you can use to create a data catalog that describes available datasets and their appropriate business applications. Lake Formation lets you define policies and control data access with simple "grant and revoke permissions to data" sets at granular levels. You can assign permissions to IAM users, roles, groups, and Active Directory users using federation. You specify permissions on catalog objects (like tables and columns) rather than on buckets and objects.

AWS Lake Formation also provides blueprints that you can run for loading and cataloging data. A blueprint allows you to import data from MySQL, Postgres, SQL Server, MariaDB, and Oracle databases running in Amazon RDS or hosted in Amazon EC2. With Lake Formation, you can import data from MySQL, Postgres, SQL Server, MariaDB, and Oracle databases running in Amazon RDS or hosted in Amazon EC2. You can also import from on-premises databases by connecting with Java Database Connectivity (JDBC).

It was indicated in the scenario that data in Parquet format is already existing in Amazon S3. As a result, you don't need to utilize a Lake Formation blueprint.

Hence, the correct answer is: Execute an AWS Glue crawler to establish a data catalog for existing data and register its Amazon S3 path location on Lake Formation. For data security, allocate granular permissions to various users.

The option that says: Leverage Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) to orchestrate and schedule data processing workflows. Ensure data security by assigning appropriate access controls is incorrect because while Amazon MWAA can orchestrate and schedule data processing workflows, it does not provide a solution for creating a data lake or managing granular access to datasets. These tasks would need to be handled separately, which could increase complexity and cost.

The option that says: Using AWS Lake Formation, register the S3 bucket where the data resides. To secure the data, assign granular permissions to different users is incorrect. You should register the Amazon S3 path of the bucket where your data is stored and not the bucket name.

The option that says: Import data from Amazon S3 using an AWS Lake Formation blueprint. Subsequently, accord users granular Lake Formation permissions as needed is incorrect because Amazon S3 is not a valid import source in a Lake Formation blueprint.

 

References:

https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/big-data/building-securing-and-managing-data-lakes-with-aws-lake-formation/

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lake-formation/latest/dg/how-it-works.html
